items.title: How to Be an Ethical Russophile
items.summary: Ask someone to name a few Russian novels, and they might rattle off the greatest hits: Anna Karenina , War and Peace , The Brothers Karamazov . Maybe they’ve read these classics and love them; maybe they just know they’re supposed to know them. Now ask the same person to name some Ukrainian novels: probably nothing. Even native Ukrainians might be more familiar with Russian books and writers than with their own literature; after the collapse of the Soviet Union, a pedestrian in Kyiv could still pass by Leo Tolstoy Square, or any number of gilded monuments to the poet Alexander Pushkin. That changed in 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Pushkin statues were razed; Tolstoy’s name was made verboten. A group of Ukrainian writers proposed a worldwide boycott of books by Russian authors. One proponent of the ban argued that “every prominent Russian name” was a way to exclude a Ukrainian. In May 2023, the free-speech nonprofit PEN America seemed to be swayed by this argument, abruptly canceling a festival panel of Russian dissident writers after protests from Ukrainian attendees. Books that merely had something to do with Russia became suspect too. Later that year, the American writer Elizabeth Gilbert announced that she’d asked her publisher to pull her forthcoming novel—a historical drama set in Siberia with no apparent relevance to the current conflict—after hearing from aggrieved readers in Ukraine. Today, such dramatic displays of solidarity are no longer in vogue. As the war grinds on and international outrage recedes, debate over cultural boycotts seems to be focused elsewhere. In May, Cannes awarded one of its top prizes to a Russian director whose anti-war film has been criticized by Ukrainians for going too easy on President Vladimir Putin. Theaters across Europe are welcoming back Russian musicians—even some with Kremlin ties —who had their performances yanked in 2022. But for the French writer Emmanuel Carrère, Russia’s cultural dominance is still a vexed subject—and a profoundly personal one. “I know, in starting this book,” he writes in the opening pages of his new memoir, Kolkhoz , “that it will deal in no small part with Ukraine and the brutal war Russia is waging there, because for me Russia, for better or worse, is a family affair.” Kolkhoz renders the history of Carrère’s Russian-émigré family in fine detail, skittering backward and forward in time, and from one vantage point to another. Throughout, he picks his way toward his major question: Is it possible for him to oppose the war and still love Russia? Carrère is best known in France for his lancing, digressive nonfiction, which often takes on controversial subjects: the 2015 Paris terrorist attacks, the lives of outlaws, his own experiences with bipolar disorder. He’s a memoirist, not a polemicist—“I prefer to rely on my experience , ” he has said —but he has an abiding interest in how individuals come to believe grand narratives and insulate themselves from truth. The 68-year-old’s “everything is copy” approach to writing has led to a few well-publicized imbroglios—as when he broke a legal agreement to write about his ex-wife in his 2020 book, Yoga , or when, in 2007’s My Life as a Russian Novel , he defied his mother, Hélène Carrère d’Encausse, a right-wing intellectual and historian of Russia, to reveal that her Georgian-born father had been a Nazi collaborator . Kolkhoz —published in France last year and newly translated into English by the discerning John Lambert—picks up on some of the threads of that family drama. This time around, he’s focused more narrowly on Hélène and her maternal relatives, whose life stories, pieced together with the help of family records collected by his father, an avid Russophile, make up the heft of the book. (Its title refers to a type of Soviet collective farm, a word that Hélène used as a playful nickname for their family unit.) Hélène was descended from a family of aristocratic “White Russians” (named for their ties to the anti-Bolshevik White Army) who were living abroad in Italy before the Russian Revolution, cosseted among servants and gardens. Carrère’s portraits of these unrepentantly bourgeois people are lively and tinged with affection—they’re Tolstoyan, in that way—but as he recounts their ordeals, he’s struck by their apparent myopia. Insurgents had been agitating against them for decades, and yet they “hadn’t seen anything coming”; the revolution arrived as a sucker punch. Once the Bolsheviks seized the family’s lands back in Russia, their fortunes evaporated. Hélène’s mother, Nathalie, ended up in Paris, along with a wave of other White Russian resettlers, defunct titles in tow. Someday, they assured one another, the Bolsheviks would be routed, and they’d be shuttled back into the highest echelons of Russian society, at the helm of a sprawling Slavic empire. Hélène, born in Paris, grew up to be a scholar of Russia’s imperial past. But she also took an interest in its trajectory after the fall of the Iron Curtain. When it became clear, in the 1990s, that a squeaky-clean republic was unlikely to magically emerge, diplomacy between Europe and the Russian Federation flagged, and Hélène saw an opening for herself. She became France’s most prominent advocate for Russia, a “regular visitor to the Kremlin” who rubbed shoulders with President Boris Yeltsin, then Vladimir Putin (she loved the perpetually drunk Yeltsin and found Putin cold but respectable), and served on the “ethics committee” for Russia Today , the state-run news network. From her perch on the French-talk-show circuit, Hélène routinely upbraided American and European leaders for humiliating Russia, which she claimed was well on its way to becoming a modern social democracy. Corruption, cronyism, a protester disappeared here or there: These were merely growing pains. Russia’s culture of hard-edged resilience would help it rightfully reassume its place among the great world powers. As for the “little people” who lived in the other post-Soviet states, including her father’s relatives in Georgia, they were “archaic, folkloric,” and largely deserving of their ancillary status. Still, Carrère notes, she never expected Russia to invade Ukraine. Just a week before the attack, with Russian troops already congregating in the Donbas, Hélène assured a TV interviewer that the country was safely off-limits. Putin, she said, was “a rational man, aware of the risks, who would never take reckless action.” Then reality proved her wrong. “I’d never heard this woman, so optimistic by nature and principle, sounding so distraught,” Carrère writes. “She kept repeating: ‘I don’t understand. I just don’t get it.’” Eventually, Hélène acknowledged the unfolding conflagration, but only to explain away her faulty reasoning—not to renounce her past statements. Putin’s motives were simply inscrutable, she insisted, even to an expert such as herself. The French media excoriated her, but she retorted that they were merely under the influence of le wokisme . Carrère returns continually to this episode throughout Kolkhoz , trying to make sense of Hélène’s intransigence. How could a woman who “prided herself on understanding the Russians” have missed the mark by so much? Why had she never interrogated her own beliefs? items.title: George Lucas spent 17 years building his latest world. This one you can walk through.
items.summary: What happens to us after we die is a fundamental question of human civilization, and anxieties about succession lurk beneath every human story: Will my work live on? Will my children pass on good values? Have I done my duty? Our rituals, religions, sacred sites, and art all seek to answer these big questions, yet none can conclusively, or we wouldn’t keep asking. I could feel these existential questions in the air as I walked past huge models of Star Wars spaceships alongside a Frida Kahlo self-portrait in the galleries of Los Angeles’ new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — a tribute to human storytelling through visual art that filmmaker George Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, a Chicago-born investor and civic leader, worked on for nearly 17 years. After a lifetime of creating and collecting exceptionally popular narrative art, what happens to these ideas and objects when their 82-year-old creator and cataloguer, George Lucas, is gone? And what happens to his reputation, his legacy — himself? I left the museum thinking that Lucas attempts to resolve the mystery of life after death in two ways. First, by guiding us through the history of visual storytelling itself and seeing how others dealt with creativity and mortality. Second, by installing his own work among high-brow canonical artists like Van Gogh, Artemisia Gentileschi, Alphonse Mucha, and Frida Kahlo. By the time we’re done with the approximately five-hour tour of the museum, we are tempted to accept Lucas’s methods and his place among the greats. Everything about this new cultural institution comes in opposing pairs. During the trippy experience of browsing this five-story museum, which houses some 100,000 square feet of gallery space, Lucas and Hobson manage to conjure an interesting co-exhibition of pop and high culture in a way that does not blur the lines between the two, but instead insists that exceptional talent and greatness exist at every level, and that each category’s leaders deserve recognition. Through curation and design, the co-founders seem to be declaring that the public, voting with its dollars, knows best. I was wondering how they did it. Credit: Anna Gát The car stops at the humbly named One Lucas Plaza. The campus is crowded, the excitement palpable. Glancing into the main lobby, you see it packed with families, the parents as keen as their kids. Upon entry, you are presented with two directions. Choosing the main lobby side on the right, you will not be done making decisions for the day. But despite always being made to choose a direction, going inside the construct that is this museum, you will be engaging with a space that has its own intentions, its own decisions, not just art. Built as a sequence of half-opening side galleries, the circular upper level seems to have been designed to make you miss things each round and need to go back and look again. I asked a museum guard where to start. “Anywhere,” he said. “It’s all a big race course.” When people first study playwriting and screenwriting, they tend to start with Aristotle. But modern dramaturgy — the art of dramatic storytelling — was founded by a later Aristotle disciple during the German Enlightenment, Gotthold Ephraim Lessing. In Laocoön (1766), Lessing sharpened the differentiation between visual and verbal art forms: visual art presents its content to the viewer all at once, with its details arranged in space, while texts such as poems unfold over time. His famous example was the mythological “Shield of Achilles.” In a painting, we receive all the shield’s details simultaneously, our eyes roaming from detail to detail. In a narrative text, this simultaneity is missing: When the same shield pops up in Homer’s Iliad , the poet doesn’t describe the finished object. Verbally, the shield can only come to life as a story, being forged by the god of blacksmiths, Hephaestus. The poet controls how we discover and imagine the shield in time. To Lessing, this fundamental difference in time, power, and agency between the two art forms raised interesting questions about theater (as this was before film): What happens when the visual and the verbal coexist in a work of art? If it took this much time and failure for a duo as powerful as Lucas and Hobson to build their museum, we should change how new cultural institutions get built in America. The curators of the Lucas Museum are fascinated with the same question but tackle it from the opposite end. How do static images — paintings, comics, statues — convey a narrative? From Moebius to Tintin to Walt Disney, through Norman Rockwell and Star Wars and Banksy, we’re asked to examine how dynamic stories are told, captured, or immortalized through what doesn’t move in front of us. Artists like George Lucas seem compelled to tell stories. In his museum, he gets to investigate his own obsession from a position of control, dictating the timeline of our discovery and how we encounter his story of stories. A mural by Banksy. Credit: Anna Gát To pull this off, the Lucas Museum presents a risky but mostly successful combination of seemingly incompatible things. In fact, everything about this new cultural institution comes in opposing pairs. What comes across as great cultural abundance — the massive museum space, the countless artworks, the library, cinema, roof garden, sculpture garden, event spaces — can all be mapped out in pairs of contrasts. Take, for instance, the building’s shape: a two-node structure informing the audience even before entry that this quest will be all about balance. The elongated “North” side houses the main lobby, the auditoriums, and the inaugural exhibition dedicated to the history of narrative art. The round “Education” side, which opens to the public gardens, houses the library (with a great view of the gardens). The galleries run above the two wings, across, all around. Credit: Lucas Museum The most crucial pair of opposites around which the Lucas Museum organizes itself is emphasized to you even before you spot the two-directionality of the building or could head upstairs. You intuit right away that pop culture and highbrow will blend here in surprising and potentially fun ways because, as you pass the glass-walled library wing on your way to the entrances, the first thing you glimpse is a life-size replica of a Naboo N-1 Starfighter ! Credit: Anna Gát Once you have recovered from this remarkable sight, you will vow to come back to the library after seeing the exhibition, and move into the main lobby on the opposite side. There, you will take a fast glass elevator upstairs, which makes some of the people inside it scream a little. And, having safely reached the gallery level, you will be thrust right into the middle of a world of fantasy and romance… That pop is the culture the exhibition starts with would have startled me somewhat had I not recently been to other LA museums, like the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. Still, accepting the unusual contrast of comics and classical art side by side does take a minute; this is not something we are visually accustomed to. Traditional museums train us to expect famous old paintings hanging from the walls. Here, images familiar from the walls of a comic book store stare back at us. Dragons and maidens, knights with swords, making a case for the contemporary human imagination. As you hop from genre to genre, from topic to topic, deeper into the museum, you eventually face Norman Rockwell classics while characters and vehicles from the Star Wars movies glare back at you through a glass partition. Credit: Anna Gát I am sure there are art purists who will be baffled or scandalized by this arrangement. items.title: Are you really who you think you are?
items.summary: Who are you? You might think you know, but science offers a more complicated answer. In fact, Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, says the inquiry may be unanswerable. A question that can be answered: Who are you in a given moment? Take, for example, someone who has a habit of interrupting while others are talking. They may see themselves as engaged — so enthusiastic that they’re compelled to interject with what they think the speaker is about to say. The person being interrupted, meanwhile, may experience their conversation partner as rude. So, do the interrupter’s intentions matter more than how they’re perceived? According to Barrett, no. The perception of rudeness is just as real — not because it matters more than the interrupter’s intentions, but because it matters just as much. “The characteristics or traits that we think are inherent to a person are not inherent to that person,” she says. “They exist to describe that person in relation to other conditions.” Your personality isn’t as fixed as it feels So, if traits are relational, then what does that mean for who we are? We often assume characteristics such as being introverted or extroverted are immovable parts of a person. According to relational realism, however, we aren’t the sole authors of our identities. Context matters. You may be extroverted when you’re interacting with people you know and you’re well-rested. You may not be so extroverted, however, when you’re in a room full of strangers and you’re hungry. “What describes you — who you are — is highly situated,” Barrett says. “As a person, that feels inherently wrong to me. But as a scientist, it seems right.” This idea violates the subjective sense many of us have that we’re made up of enduring characteristics that describe us no matter where we are and who we’re with. Science, Barrett says, doesn’t bear this out. Other people help shape who you are The human brain contains a set of patterns, and based on the statistics of the past, it begins to make an action plan for the next moment. Barrett refers to this as “meaning making.” It happens predictively and largely outside of our awareness. “Everything you do is an act of meaning making,” she says. “Even asking the question, ‘Who am I?’ and creating a story is an act of meaning making.” This process of meaning making is your Perception Box, but it doesn’t have fixed walls. Instead, it consists of a constantly fluctuating set of signals your brain uses to make sense of what’s happening in your body and the world around you. And if “who we are” emerges in part from those interactions, that means other people help shape who we are — just as we help shape them. “The logical thing to carry away here is that we have more responsibility for the identities of other people than we might think,” Barrett says. “And the people who we interact with have more influence over who we are in a moment than we might like.” Thus, one way to have more control over who we are is to take deliberate responsibility for who we interact with, and how we interact with them. When her daughter went to college, Barrett offered her this advice: Seek out people who allow you to be the best version of yourself. “Find the people who help you to be that person,” she said. “That’s the message.” We interviewed Lisa Feldman Barrett for Relational Realism , a Big Think interview series created in partnership with Unlikely Collaborators . As a creative non-profit organization, they’re on a mission to help people challenge their perceptions and expand their thinking. Often that growth can start with just a single unlikely question that makes you rethink your convictions and adjust your vantage point. Watch the fourth and final episode above, and visit Perception Box to see more in this series. This video Are you really who you think you are? is featured on Big Think .

items.summary: B ob Woodward has published a book roughly every two years since the Watergate scandal, 24 in all. Taken together, they comprise a running narrative of almost every administration from Richard Nixon’s to Donald Trump’s. The genre of the Washington book—a sequence of scenes inside rooms where important things happen, based on a convention called “deep background,” with riches of information traced to no sources—is so familiar that it’s easy to forget that Woodward practically invented it. Decade after decade, he has kept turning up in the Oval Office, at Georgetown parties, on the doorsteps of government officials—always on the job, the hunt. His approach from across a crowded room or the sudden appearance of his name on a cellphone screen has surely sunk the heart of countless sources. And yet, though they know better, they always talk, as if transfixed by a predatory stare—like the frog that agrees to carry the scorpion on its back across the lake. “Why?” the frog cries as it drowns from the inevitable sting, to which the scorpion replies: “It’s my nature.” Throughout most of Woodward’s career, several criticisms of his journalism have recurred: It provides little or no analysis; he’s a pawn of his sources, telling the story they want told; and he’s dangerous to talk to, because he privileges scoops above all else. These might seem to contradict one another, but in fact few people can survive stenography. Long quoted scenes stripped of context and meaning are almost always the cause of the damaging controversies in Woodward’s books. Once, during a panel on Iraq War reporting, the investigative reporter Seymour Hersh—perhaps the only comparable figure in American journalism, Mr. Outside to Woodward’s Mr. Inside—was asked what he thought of Woodward’s latest book about George W. Bush. The questioner was clearly baiting Hersh to denounce Woodward for shilling for the president. Instead, Hersh replied that he valued Woodward’s books because they reliably told him what was going on in the inner sanctum from which he and the rest of us were shut out. Like clockwork over the course of half a century, a Woodward book has appeared and Washington has descended into a temporary frenzy, which sometimes even resulted in political change, not least the end of a presidency. If his many best sellers endure beyond their historical moment, their relevance will be as an epic court chronicle, a contemporaneous record of an age of almost unbridled presidential power. But as his work nears an end, his kind of journalism is seeing its influence disappear. The taboos that once shamed his subjects have fallen. At 83, Woodward has had an important and interesting life, so why not write about it? But a memoir is a treacherous undertaking. “Autobiography is only to be trusted when it reveals something disgraceful,” Orwell warned. It requires an unnatural ability and willingness to explore your own dark corners, failures, humiliations. Half a century of hunting for presidential secrets didn’t prepare Woodward to be his own quarry. In Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir , he tells a few unflattering truths about himself—major stories he missed, friends he burned. But he doesn’t always grasp their full significance. Scrupulous with facts but famously unable or unwilling to reflect, he’s not a completely satisfying narrator of his own story. The best pages of VIP memoirs tend to be the early ones, before fame has arrived and revelations stiffen and grow stale. Woodward opens Secrets with scenes of self-exposure likely to startle the many sources and powerful subjects who have often experienced him as cold-blooded, risky company. Woodward was the first child of a successful lawyer and his homemaker wife in mid-century Wheaton, Illinois, strictly Republican, devoutly Christian—the most staid beginning imaginable. But his mother was emotionally unstable and unfaithful, and his father repressed his unhappiness in constant work. The atmosphere of tension and evasion gave their son a sense that his world might fall apart (since childhood, Woodward has had an acute fear of house fires). Anxiety turned him into a searcher for hidden facts: “I became a snoop. I would pry into cabinets and bedside tables, nosing through the top drawer of my father’s dresser.” At 11, Bob discovered among his father’s socks a letter from his mother referring to “our divorce”—a topic they had kept from their son. At 16, working as a janitor in his father’s law office, Bob would pilfer and pore over files of legal cases and discover scandals involving townspeople he knew. “Everybody had secrets, I realized.” This origin story explains why Woodward became not a lawyer, a professional keeper of confidences, as his father had expected, but instead a reporter who exposes them while preserving every scrap of paper that falls into his hands. To know things that others wanted to conceal gave him a sense of tenuous control in an unpredictable and dangerous world. After Wheaton came Yale, then five unhappy years in the Navy. On duty as a custodian of nuclear authentication codes, Woodward acquired the permanent fear that a nuclear war could easily happen by accident. He talked his way out of a tour in Vietnam by disingenuously claiming that, as a true Navy man, he was eager to keep serving aboard a ship. Wanting to defer law school, he talked his way into a tryout at The Washington Post . He failed in “a spectacular crash” (the concept of attribution—of identifying who said what to a reporter—was unfamiliar to him), but the speed and intensity of newspaper work were captivating. He had found the love of his life, and a year of minor-league ball with the Montgomery County Sentinel showed that he was a fast learner. In the summer of 1971, in an act of nerve that became his signature, he called the Post ’s metropolitan editor, Harry Rosenfeld, at home; got yelled at; and was given a second chance. Woodward’s account of his apprenticeship evokes the intoxicating fun of becoming a reporter with the license to go anywhere and talk with anyone. The boyish anxiety that made him spy on his parents became a professional ferocity to find out everything he could about his subjects. Woodward’s technique combines a glutton’s appetite for material, a wooer’s zeal to win over sources, and a priest’s respect for the seal of confession. The identity of “Deep Throat,” Woodward’s underground-parking-garage informant during Watergate, remained unknown to the public for more than 30 years. He turned out to be a top FBI official named Mark Felt , whom Woodward had met by chance when he was still a young Navy lieutenant, waiting in the West Wing in 1970 to deliver Pentagon documents to Henry Kissinger’s office. Felt was there on his own errand (perhaps, Woodward now speculates, to discuss Kissinger’s illegal wiretaps of aides and journalists). They chatted, and Woodward, already driven to “grab on” to anyone in Washington who might be useful, asked Felt for his phone number before they parted. The Watergate story remains an irresistible tale of youthful luck and courageous persistence. It was the first news story I ever followed closely, and whatever Woodward’s subsequent faults, to me he will always be one of the two heroes of journalism who uncovered the crimes that ended Nixon’s presidency. Woodward and Carl Bernstein’s All the President’s Men is still exhilarating—tense, vivid journalism noir, told in the third person, featuring two young reporters as its central characters. According to Secrets , this literary inspiration came from Robert Redford, who began pursuing Woodward for a movie about the pair in the fall of 1972, when the Watergate break-in was only a few months old and its historic implications unknowable. items.title: Five systems L&D can build to protect focus at work
items.summary: Many organizational cultures are out of balance. Senior leaders face an emerging tension that often goes unnoticed unless they are looking. In fact, it’s the very technology created to accelerate productivity and performance is quietly eroding both, and potentially, much more. Digital connectivity – from smartphones to social media, AI to applications – that has enabled faster decisions, global collaboration, and real-time responsiveness – has become a double-edged sword. For the myriad gains technology has delivered, we’re also paying a cognitive tax. In fact, the attention crisis, a burnout epidemic, and a degradation in decision quality are reshaping the global workforce in consequential ways. Leaders today face a paradox: leveraging technology to increase effectiveness while also protecting the health and well-being of the very people whose effectiveness they depend upon. This balance can no longer be treated as a matter of personal productivity. Digital distraction has become an organizational risk. It shapes how people think, how they feel, how they work, and how they relate to one another. Over time, it does not merely interrupt culture; it becomes culture. The costs are measurable. Task-switching on complex work can cut productivity by up to 40% , and a distraction of just three seconds can double the chance of error . But the deeper cost is to presence and trust: when leaders are only half in the room, people stop raising ideas and issues – and leaders can’t address what they don’t know about. Building the systems that manage digital distraction Managing digital distraction at scale can’t rest on individual willpower alone — it has to be designed into how the organization trains, measures, and supports its leaders. This is where leadership development plays a defining role: building the structures, norms, and programs that make focus, presence, and thoughtful responsiveness the default, not the exception. Build systems that protect focus over availability Availability and visibility have become pseudo-productivity markers in modern workplaces. But being the fastest or most frequent to reply on Slack doesn’t guarantee quality. Leadership development programs can shift this by training managers to protect and model deep, uninterrupted work as a standard, not a personal preference — embedding practices like time-blocking and response-time norms into how teams are onboarded, coached, and evaluated. Embed presence into how leaders are developed and assessed Presence is a signal that people matter. And when a team feels like the work they do matters, they’re more engaged, invested, and do their best work. Rather than leaving presence to individual temperament, leadership development can build it into manager coaching, 360 feedback, and promotion criteria — so attentiveness in interactions becomes a developed capability, not an incidental trait. Set organization-wide standards for responsiveness Speed rarely indicates quality, and yet most modern workplaces conflate a quick response with a good one. Left unaddressed, this norm sets itself team by team, inconsistently. Leadership development functions are well-placed to formalise response-time expectations and communication SLAs across the organization, teaching managers to encourage thoughtful, deliberate responsiveness rather than simply ‘fast.’ Codified this way, the standard reduces pressure to respond instantly and encourages deeper thinking, with less rework in the long run. Formalise operating principles around communication Communication norms will either be established by what’s accepted, or by what the organization intentionally designs. Leadership development can lead this work by building a shared communication charter — in collaboration with teams — that sets clear principles and boundaries around time, spaces, and channels for communication, so people can recover and get deep work done. This charter should extend to procurement and IT decisions, too: before introducing new apps and technology for ‘productivity’ gains, the organization should assess how it will impact the volume of notifications and streams employees need to manage. Build structural audits into how tools are adopted Many digital distractions are structural, not behavioral — which means the fix shouldn’t rest on individual discipline either. Leadership development, IT, and operations can jointly build a recurring audit of the volume, quality, and necessity of the digital tools teams use, reducing unnecessary apps and friction as a standing organizational practice, not a one-off. Better systems, built this way, support employees to implement tech-free boundaries sustainably. Embracing tech, with intention Digital distraction isn’t going away. Nor is it going to be solved by asking people to try harder, focus better, or show more personal discipline. The problem is cultural, which means the response must be cultural as well. And while much of the current conversation about technology has been shaped by AI, our fascination with its promise and our fear of its disruption, leaders cannot afford to overlook the subtle crisis already reshaping work. Long before generative AI entered the conversation, digital tools were fragmenting attention, accelerating false urgency, weakening presence, and making deep thought harder to sustain. AI may amplify these pressures, but it most certainly did not create them. Organizations set the conditions in which attention is either protected or constantly raided; in which responsiveness is mistaken for value or thoughtful work is given room to breathe; in which technology serves human performance or simply consumes it. Leadership development is where those conditions get built — in how managers are trained, how norms are codified, and how systems are designed. The digital leader’s paradox cannot be eliminated, but it can be led. The task is not to reject progress or retreat from the tools that make modern work possible. It is to use them with greater intention and navigate the paradox with thoughtfulness and care. Thus, preserving the focus, presence, creativity, and judgment that technology can enhance, but never replace. In a world of fragmented attention, the organizations that build the systems to cut through the noise — creating the conditions for complex thought, creativity, and togetherness — will be those who continue to thrive. items.title: In a big star-forming nebula, JWST finds the smallest failed stars
items.summary: In astronomy, the brightest objects dominate the light we receive. This image shows the central region of the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The young and dense star cluster R136 can be seen near the center of the image. The tidal forces exerted on the Large Magellanic Cloud by the Milky Way are triggering a wave of star-formation in there, which happens to be the largest star-forming region known in the Local Group. R136a1, at the cluster’s center, is the most massive single star known, with approximately 260 times the mass of our Sun. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Webb ERO Production Team When new stars form, it’s the blue supergiants that shine brightest. The same region of space, just to the right of the central bright cluster of stars in Pismis 24, shows several stars against a black background in the Hubble image (at right), but many more stars and an eerie blue haze in the JWST image (at left). The blue color is caused by the emission of neutral hydrogen atoms, recombining after being ionized by the intense ultraviolet radiation emanating from the young surrounding stars. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI, A. Pagan (STScI)/NASA, ESA and Jesús Maíz Apellániz (Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía, Spain) Alongside them, fainter, dimmer stars are much more abundant. Whereas only the brightest stars, and the star in the foreground of neutral material, are visible to primarily optical observatories like Hubble, JWST reveals bright stars, faint stars, and even background stars of the Milky Way, despite the enormous quantities and densities of gas and dust. For studying the properties and evolution of these young, massive stars, there is no better tool than JWST for the endeavor at present. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI Below the mass threshold to form stars, sub-stellar objects may yet outnumber the stars. This glowing region, filled with wispy gas, dark red dust, and brilliant blue and white stars, lies inside the nebulous star cluster Westerlund 2, located 20,000 light-years away in the constellation of Carina, toward the galactic center. With JWST, it isn’t only the bright stars that dominate, but cooler ones, brown dwarfs, and even planetary mass objects as small as the mass of several Jupiters. The infrared glow of that material, visible to JWST’s NIRCam and/or MIRI instruments, enables the detection of fainter, cooler objects than ever before. Credit : ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, V. Almendros-Abad, M. Guarcello, K. Monsch, and the EWOCS team In nebulae such as: the Cosmic Cliffs , This three-panel image shows the view of the Carina Nebula’s “cosmic cliffs” as seen by Hubble (top), JWST’s NIRCam instrument (middle), and JWST’s MIRI instrument (bottom). With its first science release in July of 2022, a new era in astronomy has truly arrived. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI; NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA) the great Orion Nebula , These two side-by-side views are centered on the Trapezium Cluster within the Orion Nebula, and show both short-infrared-wavelength (top) and long-infrared-wavelength (bottom) views of this region of space, as taken with JWST’s NIRCam imager. Credit : M.J. McCaughrean & S.G. Pearson, A&A submitted, 2023; Processing: E. Siegel and the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex , This image of the Rho Ophiuchi molecular cloud complex was released for the first science anniversary of JWST back in 2023. It showcases young stars carving out features in the surrounding star-forming material, including stellar winds and outflowing jets. Despite the apparent chaos, this is actually one of the quieter stellar nurseries known. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Klaus Pontoppidan (STScI); Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI) brown dwarfs and super-Jupiter objects appear to JWST’s eyes. Five different JuMBOs, or Jupiter-Mass Binary Objects, found within a very small region of the Orion Nebula. Note that these particular JuMBOs are numbered 31-to-35, indicating that there are dozens of these objects. Of all the Jupiter-mass objects found by this survey, about 9% of them are locked up in binary systems. Credit : M.J. McCaughrean & S.G. Pearson, A&A submitted, 2023 Within these regions, cold clouds of gas collapse, creating massive stellar seeds. This JWST image shows the large, asymmetric protostellar jet emerging from the young, star-forming region Sharpless 2-284. Located 15,000 light-years away, the protostellar jet spans an impressive 8 light-years across: driven by the most massive young star(s) and protostars within them. While some of the objects shown here are full-fledged stars, the majority of stars still within the nebulous region at the center remain in the protostellar phase, having not yet reached the main sequence as far as stellar evolution goes. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Yu Cheng (NAOJ); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars race to blow that gas away. Embedded within a cloud of gas and dust, these two nearby stars are in very different environments. The brighter, orange star is more deeply wrapped in gas and dust, and the effects of the star’s winds and radiation can be seen carving features in and evaporating the neutral matter surrounding it. In time, the surrounding, shrouding material will be evaporated away entirely. Credit : ESA/Webb, NASA, CSA, K. Luhman, C. Alves De Oliveira, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb) While the brightest stars become cosmic winners, even more losers — failed stars — persist. This zoomed-in region from JWST’s NIRCam imager shows a portion of the Orion molecular cloud complex, complete with new protostars and young protoplanetary disks. Stellar outflows and dusty, shrouded regions are all visible alongside one another, showcasing a wide range of phenomena found within star-forming regions. Credit : ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, T. Megeath, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb); Acknowledgement: M. H. Özsaraç JWST’s unique long-wavelength capabilities reveal these sub-stellar objects. Preliminary total system throughput for each NIRCam filter, including contributions from the JWST Optical Telescope Element (OTE), NIRCam optical train, dichroics, filters, and detector quantum efficiency (QE). Throughput refers to photon-to-electron conversion efficiency. By using a series of JWST filters extending to much longer wavelengths than Hubble’s limit (between 1.6 and 2.0 microns), JWST can reveal details that are completely invisible to Hubble. The more filters that are leveraged in a single image, the greater the amount of details and features that can be revealed. Credit : NASA/JWST NIRCam instrument team Within nearby nebula IC 348, 1000 light-years away in Perseus, a new record was set in 2023 . This 2023-era image from JWST shows the star-forming nebula IC 348. Searching the cluster for free-floating brown dwarfs, astronomers uncovered several objects, highlighted in the inset panels labeled 1, 2, and 3, that are less than 8 times the mass of Jupiter, including a then-record holder just 3-4 times Jupiter’s mass. For comparison, the lower mass limit for brown dwarfs was thought to be 13 solar masses, raising questions about just what these objects are and how they came to be. Credit : NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, and K. Luhman (Penn State University) and C. Alves de Oliveira (European Space Agency) A warm, glowing super-Jupiter object, just 3-4 times Jupiter’s mass, was discovered. This all-new JWST image of the nebula IC 348 extends and enhances all previous views, with the reflective interstellar material bearing many similarities to the famous “Fox Fur Nebula” and the blue region to the upper right showcasing Herbig Haro objects with plasma outflows emanating from them.
